common_name: Black Diamond Blush Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Blush-Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun and give room for an upright, tree-form habit; Blush is a softer-flowered companion to the red and white selections in the Black Diamond series.

directions: Blush pairs shell-pink flower clusters with the coppery-bronze new growth and near-black mature foliage that define the Black Diamond series, giving a softer color combination than the series' red-flowered selections. Its multi-stemmed, upright-spreading habit works well as a specimen or large hedge along a Gulf Coast property line where the dark leaves hold their color best in full sun. Water deeply through the first year or two to establish, then rely on natural rainfall except in extended drought, since established plants are quite heat and drought tolerant. Limit pruning to removing dead or crossing wood in late winter rather than heavy topping, which sacrifices next season's earliest bloom.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection / Black Diamond series

common_name: Black Diamond Purely Purple Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Purple-Flowered Crape Myrtle, PP 28,086)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun and allow room for an upright, moderately tree-like habit; Purely Purple is a patented, more recent addition to the Black Diamond series bred for true violet-purple flower color.

directions: Purely Purple carries dense clusters of vivid violet-purple flowers against near-black foliage from early summer until frost, a bloom color that stands apart from the reds and whites more typical of the Black Diamond line. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, since foliage color and flower production both fade in shade. It reblooms continuously through the Gulf Coast growing season with only light deadheading, and its upright-spreading habit trains easily into a single- or multi-trunk small tree. Prune conservatively in late winter, removing only dead, crossing, or awkward growth, since Purely Purple flowers on new wood and rarely needs hard cutback to perform well.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection / Black Diamond series

common_name: Diamond Dazzle Crapemyrtle (True Dwarf White-Flowered Crape Myrtle, PP 23,168)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Diamond Dazzle is a true dwarf, white-flowered introduction bred as a longer-blooming replacement for the earlier Snow Dazzle selection.

directions: Diamond Dazzle stays under 4 feet tall and wide, holding a dense, rounded shape that needs no hard pruning to control its size, making it a fit for foundation beds and low borders where standard crape myrtles quickly overwhelm the space. Its crisp white flower clusters open over green summer foliage that emerges reddish in spring and cover the plant more reliably through the season than older dwarf whites it was bred to replace. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and water regularly the first year to establish a deep root system. Once established it tolerates heat and drought well, needing only the removal of dead or spent wood in late winter.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivar Selection

common_name: Snow Dazzle Crape Myrtle (True Dwarf Heirloom White-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Snow Dazzle is one of the original true dwarf selections from the Dazzle breeding line, seldom exceeding 3 feet tall and wide.

directions: Snow Dazzle is among the lowest-growing crape myrtles available, forming a tight mound rarely taller than 3 feet and covered in cool white flower clusters through the heat of summer. Its compact, tidy habit suits edging, low borders, and small-space plantings where full-size crape myrtles would need constant cutting back. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil; established plants are heat and drought tolerant and need little more than occasional deep watering during prolonged dry spells. Deadhead spent clusters to extend the bloom season, and remove only dead or damaged wood in late winter.
sources: U.S. National Arboretum Lagerstroemia cultivar checklist

common_name: Delta Breeze Crapemyrtle (Lavender-Pink Dark-Foliage Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Delta Breeze is a Southern Living Plant Collection crapemyrtle bred for dark burgundy foliage and soft lavender-pink blooms.

directions: Delta Breeze bears soft lavender-pink flower clusters against curved, dark burgundy foliage, a gentler color pairing than the reds and magentas of its Delta series siblings, on a small tree that grows taller and narrower than most dwarf crape myrtles. It is heat-tolerant and generally resists deer browsing better than many other landscape shrubs, making it a good fit along Gulf Coast property lines and streetscapes. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season. Prune lightly in late winter to remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches rather than heavily topping the plant.
